We are investigating a recurring memory-cgroup OOM kill on our OLK-6.6 production fleet (kernel 6.6.0-21.0.0.21.oe2403.x86_64). The pattern is the java workload triggering memcg OOM via the page-fault filemap charge path. Around the same time the security team flagged CVE-2024-26926 mentioning memcg charge accounting, and our backport-tracking script proposed upstream commit 892962a26026 (mm: memcontrol: don't throttle dying tasks on memory.high) as a candidate fix.

Please walk our FULL diagnostic workflow end-to-end so we can produce a complete investigation report:

  1. Parse the dmesg and extract the call trace structure; check taint flags.
  2. Phase 0 — hash the call-trace signature and look up similar past crashes (syzbot, Bugzilla, LKML).
  3. Phase 1 — reverse-lookup commits touching mem_cgroup_out_of_memory, try_charge_memcg, __filemap_get_folio, out_of_memory, oom_kill_process. Also expand from those symbols (callers / callees / related identifiers) and read the source of one frame.
  4. Phase 2 — BM25 keyword search across commits, LKML mail threads, Bugzilla bugs, syzbot crashes, the CVE database, and the kernel source tree for terms like "memcg charge accounting OOM kill".
  5. Phase 3 — browse recent fixes in the mm / memcg subsystem.
  6. Phase 4 (mandatory) — for commit 892962a26026: fetch its full body, fetch its diff, run get_regression_fixes (was it reverted? does it itself fix a regression?), check whether it is already in OLK-6.6 vs OLK-5.10, look up MAINTAINERS owner of mm/memcontrol.c, and check whether this commit fixed any known syzbot crash.
  7. Cross-check the CVE: pull CVE-2024-26926 details and see whether OLK-6.6 already carries its fix.
  8. Produce a final report: which commits to backport (or which to avoid because of a revert chain), the maintainer pointer, and confidence calibration. If KG returns nothing definitive, fall back to first-principles reasoning about memcg charge edge cases and say so explicitly.

Goal: exercise every KG path we have. This is a smoke test for tool coverage; the depth of analysis matters more than the speed.
